prompt.context: Sergeant Slaughter's Construction Company is a leading provider of construction and infrastructure materials. It has two divisions: Oil & Gas and Government. The government division's main customer is the US Military. Your client is offering construction services to help the US military to build bases. Construction includes dining facilities, dorms, and infrastructure projects for troops around the world. Each division has its own procurement department. The procurement for the government division spends $6 billion on the items they purchase. They resell those items for a profit to the Government.
prompt.question: The Vice President of procurement for the government division called your consulting firm to advise them on how to spend less money on the purchased items and operate more efficiently. How would you approach this problem?

clarifying_info.q: What kind of contracts does the government division have with its supplier — long-term or short-term?
clarifying_info.a: Contracts between suppliers and the Government division are short-term in nature.

clarifying_info.q: How many suppliers does the government division use?
clarifying_info.a: The company has only one supplier. The supplier offers the best cost/quality ratio and Sgt. Slaughter would like to keep it if possible. The client is not the only customer for the supplier but is one of the largest.

clarifying_info.q: Is there competition for the government contract?
clarifying_info.a: The company is the main supplier for the Government. They are the best at what they do and do not need to worry about competition as long as they maintain present prices and quality.

clarifying_info.q: How experienced is the procurement staff?
clarifying_info.a: The staff is not the most experienced. The VP of Procurement is a newly hired former lawyer. Workers spend most of their time troubleshooting and enforcing contracts rather than negotiating.

clarifying_info.q: What is the productivity target vs. actual productivity of workers?
clarifying_info.a: The target is 88% productivity (of billed time) but workers are only productive 80% of the time billed. There are no training or learning processes in place. The bonus structure is fixed: a 10% undifferentiated bonus at year-end if the company makes a profit.

clarifying_info.q: Does the Oil & Gas division use the same supplier? How large are their orders?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the same supplier. The Oil & Gas division accounts for $2 billion in orders from suppliers.

clarifying_info.q: Do the two divisions collaborate or share information?
clarifying_info.a: The Government division does not communicate efficiently with the Oil & Gas division. They have issues integrating data and do not have a common database with prices across the globe and former experiences.

framework: 1. Contractual relationship with suppliers and the Government — contract type, duration, leverage
2. Workforce efficiency — experience, productivity, incentives, training
3. Inter-division synergies — collaboration between Government and Oil & Gas procurement
4. Information flow and technology — shared data systems, common database, demand forecasting

questions.prompt: What information do we need to understand the nature of the business relationship between suppliers and the Government?
questions.guidance: Strong answers explore: contract type (long-term vs short-term) and trade-offs; demand volatility (e.g., if the Iraq war ends, demand could drop sharply making long-term contracts risky); number of suppliers and diversification options; Sgt. Slaughter's competitive position. Candidate should infer that a single supplier creates concentration risk and that demand volatility makes long-term contracts a double-edged sword requiring a negotiated exit clause.

questions.prompt: Given the supplier and contract situation, what proposals would you make to improve procurement cost efficiency?
questions.guidance: Proposals should include: (1) identify multiple suppliers or use that possibility as bargaining leverage against the current one; (2) negotiate long-term contracts for better pricing but include a 'call clause' (exit option) if government demand drops; (3) identify synergies with the Oil & Gas division to increase combined bargaining power. Note: candidate cannot negotiate a better price from the government — proposals must focus on the supply side.

questions.prompt: What organizational questions should we ask about the people in the procurement department?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates ask about: experience levels of negotiators; incentive structures; staffing model and productivity; training and development programs. Key data: target productivity is 88% but actual is 80% of billed time; VP is a newly hired former lawyer with limited procurement experience; workers focus on contract enforcement rather than negotiation; bonus is a flat 10% undifferentiated year-end payment tied only to company profit.

questions.prompt: What proposals would you make to improve workforce efficiency in procurement?
questions.guidance: Proposals: (1) hire more experienced procurement/negotiating staff; (2) offer formal training programs; (3) redesign incentives — tie bonuses to money saved from suppliers rather than flat profit-sharing; (4) reduce workforce if warranted and implement productivity monitoring to raise actual productivity from 80% to the 88% target; (5) shift worker focus from contract enforcement toward active supplier negotiation.

questions.prompt: How can Sgt. Slaughter leverage synergies between the Government and Oil & Gas divisions?
questions.guidance: Candidate should probe: do divisions use the same supplier (yes); combined spend is $6B + $2B = $8B — substantially larger than either division alone; are the divisions coordinating (no — data integration issues exist). Proposals: (1) coordinate orders between divisions to increase combined bargaining power over shared supplier; (2) institute a common demand-forecasting and ordering system; (3) build a shared global database of negotiated prices and supplier experiences; (4) organize joint procurement meetings to share best practices; (5) consider merging the two procurement departments into one company-wide unit.

math.setup: Government division spend: $6B. Oil & Gas division spend: $2B. Combined spend if consolidated: $6B + $2B = $8B.
math.answer: Consolidated procurement would negotiate from a $8 billion spend base vs. $6 billion alone — a 33% increase in purchasing leverage.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the levers Sgt. Slaughter can pull to reduce procurement costs and improve efficiency?

categories.name: Supplier Relationships
ideas: Identify and qualify additional suppliers to create competitive tension
Negotiate long-term contracts with volume discounts
Include call/exit clauses in long-term contracts to manage demand volatility
Use combined Oil & Gas + Government spend ($8B) as bargaining chip

categories.name: Workforce & People
ideas: Replace flat bonus with savings-linked incentive (% of cost reduction achieved)
Implement productivity tracking to close the 80% vs. 88% gap
Shift worker time from contract enforcement to proactive negotiation

categories.name: Organizational Structure
ideas: Merge Government and Oil & Gas procurement into one company-wide department
Share best practices between divisions through regular joint meetings

categories.name: Technology & Information
ideas: Build a common global database of supplier prices and contract history
Integrate demand forecasting data across both divisions
Implement shared procurement platform to coordinate purchase orders
Use data analytics to optimize order timing and volumes

recommendation: To reduce procurement costs, Sgt. Slaughter should consolidate the Government and Oil & Gas procurement departments into a single unit, leveraging their combined $8 billion spend to negotiate better terms with their shared supplier.
Workforce changes are urgent: hire experienced negotiators, implement procurement training, and tie bonuses to cost savings rather than company-wide profit to align incentives.
On contracts, negotiate long-term agreements with the supplier to secure volume pricing, but include a demand-contingent exit clause given the volatility of government military spending.
risks: Government demand could fall sharply (e.g., end of military operations), making long-term supplier contracts a liability without a call clause
Relying on a single supplier remains a concentration risk even with better contracts; diversification should be explored over time
Merging procurement departments may face organizational resistance and short-term productivity disruption
next_steps: Conduct a spend analysis across both divisions to quantify full negotiating leverage
Issue RFPs to at least two alternative suppliers to establish competitive benchmarks
Design a revised incentive structure linking procurement bonuses to measurable cost savings
Assess IT systems and scope a shared procurement database and demand-forecasting tool
Develop a transition plan for potential consolidation of the two procurement departments
